title: Microscope Slides in Motion — source and archive registry supplement 08

records.collection: Historical microscope-slide and histology collections, including Darwin and Balfour material
records.type: historical slide collection + collector catalogues/notebooks + original cabinets
records.holdings: The Museum states that many historical collections arrived with collectors' own catalogues and notebooks and that some remain together in original cabinets. It specifically identifies Charles Darwin's barnacle microscope slides and Francis Maitland Balfour's embryological serial sections as collections of exceptional historical importance. The broader histology collection contains serially sectioned vertebrate material, while the Museum reports roughly 300 Darwin barnacle slides.
records.research_use: A high-value object↔paper route in which original cabinet order, collector documentation, serial sectioning and publication can potentially be studied together. Balfour is especially useful for connecting microscope slides to microtome technique, embryological sequence and printed research; Darwin offers a separate slide↔monograph relation.
records.access: Collections database and collection histories are online; research access by enquiry to the University Museum of Zoology.

records.institution: Whipple Museum of the History of Science / Department of Zoology, University of Cambridge
records.collection: Francis Maitland Balfour microscope objectives, microtome equipment, and associated Zoology collections
records.holdings: The Whipple Museum records microscope objectives and accessories used by Francis Maitland Balfour, including Zeiss and Gundlach objectives, with provenance from the Department of Zoology. It also preserves a Rudolf Jung sliding microtome from the 1870s transferred from Zoology. Cambridge departmental histories connect Balfour and his circle to the development and use of serial-section microtomy and note the survival of Balfour's embryological sections in the Museum of Zoology.
records.research_use: Direct apparatus↔slide route for reconstructing how an embryological serial section was produced and read. The surviving objectives, microtome, slide series and publication captions offer a bounded test of whether instrument acquisition can be linked to particular preparations or printed plates.
records.access: Whipple object records and images online; research through the Whipple Museum and Department/Museum of Zoology.

records.institution: University of Manchester — Museum of Medicine and Health
records.collection: A. R. Gibson Victorian microscope-slide cabinet
records.type: historical private slide cabinet + tray-level research documentation
records.date_scope: slides from 1862; principally late nineteenth century
records.holdings: The Gibson collection is a wooden cabinet of numbered trays containing Victorian microscope slides. University research describes 25 numbered trays with roughly 24–30 slides per tray and a tray-by-tray report; labels commonly preserve taxon, supplier, locality and preparation date. Recorded makers and suppliers include firms in London, Liverpool, Manchester and Southport.
records.research_use: A ready-made object pool for reversing the project's trade-catalogue research into surviving labels. Numbered tray coordinates, supplier names, dates and subjects make it possible to test how commercial maker identities remained legible in a private cabinet and later museum catalogue.
records.access: Research access through the Museum of Medicine and Health; University articles expose sample labels, makers, slide coordinates and photomicrographs.

records.type: university teaching collection + historical microscope slides + documents
records.date_scope: museum founded 1887; historical slides include Walter Baldwin Spencer and departmental researchers
records.holdings: The Tiegs Museum, founded in 1887, preserves an extensive microscope-slide collection with contributions from Walter Baldwin Spencer and other former departmental researchers. The museum also retains reprints and other historical documents of cultural significance alongside its zoological teaching specimens.
records.research_use: A southern-hemisphere university comparator for following slide production and teaching inside a department founded in the late nineteenth century. Named Spencer material and associated historical documents create a route from departmental practice to surviving preparations without beginning from British society exchange.
records.access: Research through the Tiegs Museum and School of BioSciences, University of Melbourne.

records.institution: University of Melbourne — Medical History Museum / University Archives
records.collection: Henry J. Grayson ruling-engine material and William Stone archival route
records.type: instrument history + photographic record + associated scientist archive
records.holdings: University of Melbourne collections preserve photographs of Henry J. Grayson with his micro-ruling engine, while the final Grayson ruling engine remained in the University's Department of Natural Philosophy. An Australian science-archives account records that Grayson's research notebooks and papers were destroyed shortly after his death, in contrast to the surviving William Stone archive, which documents later work around the ruling engine and scientific practice.
records.research_use: Important negative-control case for the test-plate/metrology project. It shows how the survival of an instrument and photographs, combined with destruction of the maker's papers, constrains reconstruction of the relation between ruling practice, commercial test slides and later users. Stone's papers offer a downstream archival route rather than a substitute for Grayson's lost archive.
records.access: Museum and University Archives research by arrangement; collection and archive descriptions are online.

records.institution: Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg — Institute for the History of Medicine / Anatomy collections
records.collection: Historical histology collection with sections by Albert von Kölliker
records.holdings: The Würzburg medical-history collections explicitly retain the Anatomy Institute's histology collection, whose oldest sections are still attributed to Albert von Kölliker. University collection histories also identify Kölliker as a leading nineteenth-century histologist who introduced microscopy courses and helped build Würzburg's anatomical teaching infrastructure.
records.research_use: A rare surviving route into mid-nineteenth-century histology teaching at an institution central to microscopy and cellular anatomy. The key next step is to recover the historical catalogue, preparation labels and any course or institute records that connect Kölliker's sections to lectures, methods and publications.
records.access: Collection consultation by arrangement with the Institute for the History of Medicine / Anatomy collections.

records.collection: Costa Simões histology course, microscope-preparation catalogue, physiology apparatus, and visual documentation
records.type: historical teaching catalogue + institutional visual archive
records.date_scope: 1872–1873 catalogue; later nineteenth/early twentieth-century institute documentation
records.holdings: A. A. da Costa Simões published in 1873 a programme for the University of Coimbra chair of Histology and General Physiology together with a catalogue of its collection of microscopic preparations and experimental-physiology apparatus, illustrated with 92 original engravings. Coimbra's historical-science digital collections also preserve an early photograph of the Histology room with microscopes, and later institutional bibliography identifies documentary series concerning the Histology Institute and its microscopes.
records.research_use: A strong institutional comparator to Tokyo. Here the course programme, microscopic-preparation collection and physiology apparatus were formally catalogued together, allowing teaching content, object inventory and instruments to be analysed as one designed pedagogical system even if survival of the original 1873 slides still requires verification.
records.access: The 1873 catalogue is digitally available; Coimbra historical-science and library collections provide further institutional records and images.

records.collection: Ernst Haeckel online correspondence — microscopic preparations, radiolarian slides, specimen exchange and preparator trade
records.holdings: The critical online Haeckel correspondence exposes searchable TEI texts and archival metadata. Slide-relevant letters include a recipient thanking Haeckel in 1896 for a Radiolaria collection of small glass slides intended for microscopic viewing, as well as broader correspondence documenting specimen shipments, preparation work, exchange and purchase from professional preparators.
records.research_use: A direct primary-source search environment for reconstructing how microscopic preparations moved as gifts, research materials and purchasable objects around Haeckel's zoological work. It can be queried systematically for Präparat, Mikroskop, Glastäfelchen, Radiolarien, Objektträger, Versand, Ankauf and named preparators, then connected to surviving Jena collections where possible.
records.access: Open searchable online edition with TEI text, metadata, signatures and citation information.

records.collection: Victorian microscope slides in the Zoology Museum / D'Arcy Thompson collections
records.holdings: University of Dundee collection pages publish examples of Victorian microscope slides, including a Watson & Sons arrangement of named foraminifera and a numbered marine-zoology series prepared by Hornell & Sinel, alongside other zoological slides. University exhibitions have also used D'Arcy Thompson's own microscope slides and documentary collections.
records.research_use: A compact object-level route for testing named commercial and specialist series against catalogues and periodical evidence. Watson & Sons and Hornell & Sinel provide immediately searchable maker anchors, while D'Arcy Thompson material offers a separate research/teaching afterlife.
records.access: Collection pages and images online; research access through University of Dundee Museum Collections.
